questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by its index in an array list?

feedback.text: Correct — the address is computed directly from the base plus index.
No traversal is needed; the index gives the address directly.
There is no binary search involved in indexing.
That is a sorting cost, unrelated to indexed access.

generalfeedback.text: Contiguous storage lets an index map to a memory address in constant time.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of inserting or deleting an element in the middle of an array list?

feedback.text: Correct — the following elements must be shifted to close or open a gap.
Only appending at the end can be O(1); middle edits shift elements.
Shifting is linear, not logarithmic.
A single middle insertion shifts at most n elements, so O(n).

generalfeedback.text: Because storage is contiguous, a middle insert or delete must shift the trailing elements, costing O(n).

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of appending an element to the end of a dynamic array list?

feedback.text: Correct — most appends are O(1), and occasional resizes average out.
Only the rare resizing append is O(n); most are O(1).
Appending does not involve a logarithmic search.

answer.text: Strict O(1) worst case for every append

feedback.text: The occasional resize makes a single append O(n) in the worst case, hence amortized O(1).

generalfeedback.text: Appends are O(1) until the array fills; a resize costs O(n) but is infrequent, giving amortized O(1).

questiontext.text: When a dynamic array runs out of capacity, how does it typically grow?

answer.text: It allocates a new array of double the capacity and copies the elements over

feedback.text: Correct — geometric (doubling) growth gives amortized O(1) appends.

answer.text: It grows by exactly one slot each time an element is added

feedback.text: Growing by one makes every append O(n) overall; doubling is used instead.

answer.text: It halves its capacity to save memory

feedback.text: Halving on a full array would lose data; capacity must grow.

answer.text: It converts itself into a linked list of nodes

feedback.text: A dynamic array reallocates a larger array; it does not become a linked list.

generalfeedback.text: Doubling the capacity on overflow spreads the O(n) copy cost across many O(1) appends.

questiontext.text: Which statements about an array list are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Elements are stored contiguously in memory

feedback.text: Yes — that is what enables O(1) indexing.

answer.text: Random access by index is O(1)

feedback.text: Yes — the address is computed directly.

answer.text: Inserting in the middle is O(1)

feedback.text: No — it is O(n) because trailing elements shift.

answer.text: It never needs to move elements when appending

feedback.text: No — a resize copies all elements to a larger array.

generalfeedback.text: Array lists give O(1) indexed access via contiguous storage, but middle edits shift and resizes copy.

questiontext.text: An array list provides O(1) random access to any element by its index.

feedback.text: Correct — contiguous storage maps an index to an address directly.
Indexed access is indeed O(1) for an array list.

questiontext.text: Inserting an element in the middle of an array list is an O(1) operation.

feedback.text: The trailing elements must shift, making it O(n).
Correct — a middle insert shifts elements and costs O(n).

questiontext.text: In an array list you access an element directly by its numeric ______.

feedback.text: Correct — the index maps to a memory address in O(1).
Correct — the index maps to a memory address in O(1).
